items.originalTitle: Democrats see an immigration opening despite Stephen Miller’s rise
items.author: Samuel Benson, Myah Ward and Eric Bazail-Eimil
items.title: Democrats see an immigration opening despite Stephen Miller’s rise
items.summary: In the days before the midterm election, Rep. Henry Cuellar (D-Texas) felt confident that a blue wave could open the door to immigration reform. Cuellar was so bullish that he reached out to acting Immigration and Customs Enforcement director David Venturella and the Customs and Border Protection commissioner Rodney Scott to feel out areas of “common ground,” he said in an interview. Now Cuellar is one of several moderate Democrats angling to strike a deal with the White House, especially on reining in ICE officers and creating legal pathways to citizenship for some immigrants. They’re undeterred by President Donald Trump’s elevation of immigration hardliner Stephen Miller to chief of staff. And they’re buoyed by Trump’s recent admission that his deportations policy was “too tough.” Several of these Democrats have already placed calls to Trump and DHS secretary Markwayne Mullin to express a willingness to work together. Cuellar said he reached back out to Venturella and Scott after the election to try to schedule meetings. “If the president, as the president of the United States, makes a decision — and not a chief of staff — we can get the job done,” Cuellar said in an interview. “I’m sure we’re going to find a lot of differences, but if we sit down, we can definitely resolve them.” It’ll be a tough road: Securing buy-in from the White House becomes undoubtedly more complicated with Miller, a champion of the administration’s aggressive deportation push. Republicans in Congress have largely been willing to defer to the president on the issue. And Democratic leaders have questioned Trump’s sincerity and said they have no interest in working with Miller. The possibility will become even more tenuous once Democrats begin investigating the Trump administration, including the president’s immigration enforcement agencies. CBP and ICE did not respond to requests for comment. Neither did Democratic leaders Sen. Chuck Schumer and Rep. Hakeem Jeffries. Democrats like Cuellar, Sen.-elects James Talarico of Texas and Annie Andrews of South Carolina are aware of all of those hurdles. But they’re betting the midterms have created an opening for serious talks: Latino voters across the country swung hard back toward Democrats this cycle, and more and more Republicans are recognizing that their immigration agenda hurt them politically. Talarico and Andrews have publicly expressed interest in working with the president on immigration, and both ran on platforms that emphasized creating paths to citizenship for undocumented immigrants. “I’m ready to work with President Trump to fix this broken immigration system,” Talarico said in a statement. Inside the White House, there’s a recognition that the president will proceed however he so chooses, regardless of who the chief of staff is. Trump is accessible to outside voices — journalists, business leaders and lawmakers regularly call him directly — and often poses policy questions to aides and allies as he decides which direction he will go. “Everybody’s like, ‘Well, it’s never going to happen with Stephen Miller.’ Look, Donald Trump’s the president. I don’t care if Stephen Miller’s the chief of staff or Susie Wiles or John Kelly or whoever the chief of staff might be,” said a person close to the White House, granted anonymity to speak about the internal dynamic. For Democrats, there’s a real political incentive to getting a deal done ahead of a critical 2028 presidential election — especially as the party seeks to win back voter trust on immigration and border security, policy areas that spelled doom for them in 2024. “You have these Democrats who flip red states, and it’s also to their self-interest, right? Not just to do rhetoric, and go big or go home, but actually come to the middle with the president, with the Republicans. Because if not, I think that the big lesson this election is, Hispanic voters are gonna flip back ... if they don’t see Democrats delivering anything the next two years,” said Rebecca Shi, the executive director of ABIC, a coalition of pro-immigration reform business executives. She added that there’s a lesson for Republicans, too, if they don’t come to the table: “They will lose the White House.” White House spokesperson Lauren Bis touted Trump’s immigration accomplishments, including border security, a drop in crime and the creation of the Homeland Security Task Force and said the president’s “strong immigration policy remains unchanged.” She said Democrats should work alongside Trump to “keep our southern border secure, remove dangerous illegal criminals from our communities, and stop the illicit trafficking of lethal drugs.” Democrats welcomed the president’s remarks on 60 Minutes on Sunday, when he said he was open to legal pathways for some unauthorized immigrants who haven’t committed crimes and are working and contributing to the economy. Mullin also floated an openness to a bipartisan immigration overhaul involving DACA, which could provide permanent legal status to some undocumented immigrants who arrived in the U.S. as children, even as he — and the president — have insisted that any proposal wouldn’t include amnesty. In a sign that Democrats have learned the lessons of the Biden administration , many of them are eager to pair reforms with border security measures. Cuellar, who will chair the Homeland Security Appropriations subcommittee in the next conference, has long suggested including guardrails on ICE in the next funding bill, such as requiring judicial warrants, rolling out body camera usage and restoring “sensitive locations” such as churches and schools as off-limits. Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.), another Democrat who has expressed interest in working with the Trump administration, said that beyond “talk,” it would help to see some smaller concrete policy shifts from the White House to affirm that Trump is, in fact, open to changes to the immigration system. “The way to do that is to have some reforms already at ICE — whether it’s shutting down these detention centers, giving certain level of protections, whether to veterans, so they don't get deported, to maybe parents of U.S. citizens, they don’t get deported — something to show that, you know, it's not just talk, this isn’t going to be a policy led by Stephen Miller,” he said. But Miller remains a bogeyman for Democrats, someone they view as responsible for the president’s most extreme immigration policies. As chief of staff, he can ensure he’s one of the last people in the president’s ear — and that the White House doesn’t bend to what he sees as unrealistic Democratic demands. “The reason why they wouldn’t do an amnesty deal, I believe, is because it would be the ultimate and most public contradiction of the central thesis of this entire political program as it was sold to voters,” said Mike Howell, president of the Oversight Project and a member of the Mass Deportation Coalition. “It would be the end of the America First coalition as it currently exists.” Democrats' distrust of Miller will also make it challenging for them to align on any potential deal with the White House. “Stephen Miller is the mastermind and architect of terror, and death, and illegality in this country, and he is not anyone who even understands truthfully what immigration policy should look like,” said Rep. Sydney Kamlager-Dove (D-Calif). “No deals, man. No deals,” she added. The White House pointed to Miller’s experience on the Hill as a valuable asset. White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers said unlike Democrats “who refused to work with the President and blocked many of his popular policies, Stephen Miller has a track record of spearheading bipartisan efforts: public safety reform, making our cities such as Washington, D.C. and Memphis safe again, drug pricing transparency, and unleashing a nuclear energy renaissance.” Lawmakers are waiting for the president to make the first move. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, who will continue to lead his fellow Republicans when Democrats retake control of the Senate this January, told reporters after the election that “if there's something he wants to do there, we can have that conversation.” “There are always some landmines, which is why in the past the wheels have kind of come off, despite some really good efforts at trying to find a landing spot. But yeah we're open to something he wants to propose,” Thune added. Jordain Carney contributed to this report.

items.originalTitle: AI Is Giving Optical Computing Another Shot
items.author: Dina Genkina
items.title: AI Is Giving Optical Computing Another Shot
items.summary: The idea of computing with light has been around for over 70 years, but until recently it’s remained largely in the realm of research. Over the past few years, though, optical computing has emerged as a fast-growing industry: Market valuation of companies in this sector now totals US $2.22 billion, up from $0.4 billion in 2022. One projection suggests that the market will continue to grow exponentially in the coming years. The reason for this sudden surge will surprise no one: AI. In particular, AI inference—the process of using AI models to respond to user queries—has driven much of the construction of huge, power-hungry data centers, and relatively energy-efficient optical systems are seen as a potential way forward. “Most of the interest in [photonics] is driven by the fact that AI inference has literally become limited by power, and in a rather striking manner,” says Peter McMahon , associate professor of applied and engineering physics at Cornell University, in Ithaca, N.Y., who has researched optical computing for over a decade. Optics, at least on paper, carries the promise of doing the same math as today’s GPUs at a drastically lower level of power. Switching from electronics to optics would be a pretty radical solution. Nevertheless, like mushrooms after a rainstorm, optical-computing startups are popping up in the United States, China, Germany, and Israel. And while competing against such GPU makers as Nvidia is an ambitious goal, the investment in optical computing has spurred development of complementary approaches, such as designing alternative AI algorithms, taking on scientific computing, and enhancing in-network computing. Optalysys, based in England, is inserting optical-computing elements into the networking path, where data centers already use light. The company’s basic on-chip optical element, shown in the inset, is a Fourier transform calculator. Optalysys “I think it would be good for the technology if many of these companies made a good run at it,” says Logan Wright , assistant professor of applied physics at Yale University, in New Haven, Conn., and a former postdoc in McMahon’s lab. “I think that the technology that will be developed through this would be really, really useful, and enable photonic systems that maybe don’t get on this wave of AI but would be capable of doing really quite special things.” Optics to inference’s rescue? Inference makes up the bulk of AI energy use. The industry is already spending billions of dollars designing advanced GPUs and other chips to run inference as efficiently as possible. At the heart of the inference computation is one operation, done countless times a second: matrix-vector multiplication. Back in 1978, optical-computing pioneer Joseph W. Goodman and his coworkers proposed a method for doing matrix-vector multiplication with light. The setup was relatively simple. Let’s say a vector of length N needs to be multiplied by a matrix of size N by N . N light-emitting diodes, all in a row, encode the elements of the vector into the intensity of light—the brighter the light from an individual diode, the greater the value that diode encodes. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads out the light vertically, essentially copying the vector N times. The light then passes through an attenuator of N by N pixels. At each pixel, the light is attenuated according to the corresponding value at that location in the matrix. Passing the light through the attenuator performs the multiplication. Finally, a cylindrical lens oriented perpendicular to the first lens re-collects the light from each row, summing it up. The final vector is measured by a row of detectors. VECTOR-MATRIX MULTIPLICATION The most computationally expensive part of common AI today is vector-matrix (or matrix-matrix) multiplication. For a vector of length N (here, N = 3), it takes N 2 (here, 9) multiplication steps and three accumulation steps—multiple additions at once. The argument for why optics might be advantageous over electronics goes something like this: Multiplying a matrix of size N by N by a vector of length N takes N 2 multiplication steps. In electronics, each multiplication takes some energy, so the total energy used scales as N 2 . In optics, however, the multiplication step is passive: As long as the matrix stays the same, passing light through the attenuator costs almost no energy. The only cost is encoding the vector into light and reading out the answer, but the vector is of length N , not N 2 . So the energy used will scale as N , not N 2 , as bigger vectors and matrices are multiplied. Since Goodman’s 1978 proposal, the quality of the available optical elements has improved dramatically. Indeed, in 2022, a team of researchers at Cornell led by McMahon demonstrated an optical neural network that consumed less than one photon of energy—approximately 2.5 x 10 -19 joules—per multiplication operation. In a standard computer, a single multiply operation can take between 10 -14 and 10 -12 joules, which suggests that optics could possibly reduce energy use by a factor of 100,000. But McMahon cautions against such extrapolation. First, the cost of encoding data into optics was not included in the calculation. Even if the scaling is favorable with light, in practice it’s not just the scaling that matters, it’s also the coefficients. Let’s say the energy cost of doing one multiplication with electronics is 1 picojoule, and the cost to encode one vector element with optics is 1,000 picojoules. The electronic approach still wins if the length N of the vector is fewer than 1,000 elements. McMahon says this example is not far off from reality: “One of the key questions is, How big do you have to make the system before you start winning? Lots of people have done this calculation for various kinds of neural networks. The very rough answer is somewhere between N equals 1,000 and N equals 10,000.” It’s also important to keep in mind a computing principle known as Amdahl’s law . “Amdahl’s law shouldn’t even be called a law. It’s a simple piece of common sense,” McMahon says. “If you have something that’s going to accelerate a computation, and it can accelerate 90 percent of the code, but there’s 10 percent of the code that it can’t accelerate, then the maximum possible speedup you can get is 10x.” With AI inferencing, the point is to save energy, not time. But Amdahl’s observation still applies. What fraction of today’s AI inferencing code can be better handled with optics is a complicated question that varies by approach. But it’s not 100 percent. Matrix-vector multiplication, or matrix-matrix multiplication, is only part of the inference workload—there are other, nonlinear operations that need to be performed on the data. Taking all of these caveats into account, optical-computing companies today are aiming for a 10- to 80-fold improvement in energy efficiency over today’s GPUs. The question is whether they can deliver on that promise at scale before traditional electronics catches up to those gains. Bridging the gap in free space The startup Lumai , based in Oxford, England, has taken perhaps the most direct inspiration from Goodman and his team. Lumai’s head of product, Phillip Burr , declares that a free-space approach, where the light travels through air rather than on-chip waveguides, is what will enable the company’s tech to beat GPUs. Instead of the fixed attenuator used in Goodman’s proposal, Lumai is using a modern programmable device called a spatial light modulator—a pixelated membrane akin to a fancy liquid-crystal display that can modulate both the intensity and phase of light. The rest of the design is more sophisticated in practice but similar in principle to Goodman’s design: A vector is encoded into light, copied N times via a lens, passed through the spatial light modulator, collected with another lens, and the result is converted back to digital electronics. The electronics then handle the nonlinear functions. “A full vector-matrix multiply completes in a single optical cycle,” Burr says. To accurately compare the energy expenditures of the optical and GPU approaches, you must first specify which part of the workload you’re considering. Modern inference is often split into two phases: prefill , where the input query is processed and propagated through the model, and decode , where the output is generated one word (or token) at a time. Prefill is the more computationally intensive of the two. It basically involves doing vector-matrix multiplications for the same matrix over and over. Decode also involves vector-matrix multiplies, but not as intensively—the time-consuming part of decode is reading the necessary matrices in and out of memory. Vector-matrix multiplication with free-space optics The Goodman optical computer is the simplest version of a photonic vector-matrix multiplier. Here, the vector elements are encoded into the intensity of light from three light sources, such as LEDs. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads the light vertically. The matrix elements are encoded into the opacity of an attenuator, such that when light passes through each pixel it is multiplied (attenuated) by that matrix value. Finally, another cylindrical lens collects the light horizontally, performing the accumulation step, and a photodetector measures the output vector. Lumai, and other companies in the space, are focusing on the compute-intensive prefill phase of inference. Lumai claims that its Iris Nova optical server, made available for evaluation in April 2026, is a proof of concept, and its next-generation Iris Aura server will do prefill using roughly one-tenth of the energy a GPU would use. The startup Neurophos , based in Austin, Texas, is putting a different spin on the Goodman computer design. To pack more punch into a small device, the company is leveraging its expertise in metamaterials—complex structures that can manipulate light at scales smaller than a single wavelength. The structures it has designed are bigger than a wavelength but still quite small—just several micrometers per side. “The equivalent of the optical transistor that you can get from standard silicon photonics today is like 2 millimeters long,” says Patrick Bowen , CEO of Neurophos. “You just can’t fit enough [of] them on-chip to get a compute density that remotely competes with the latest and greatest [that] TSMC [Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.] does.” Bowen’s team designed metamaterial-based modulators that can be programmed to manipulate the phase and intensity of light at the micrometer scale, resulting in an array of 1,000 by 1,000 modulators in a square chip with 5-mm sides. According to Bowen, Neurophos’s modulators switch over 10,000 times as fast as a standard liquid-crystal spatial light modulators do. Bowen also claims a performance advantage over Nvidia’s Blackwell GPU: “We’re targeting 50 times Blackwell B200’s speed and 35 times its energy efficiency, and have a road map to reach 250 times the speed and roughly 90 times the energy efficiency in subsequent generations.” The approach is CMOS-compatible, Bowen says, which should allow Neurophos to manufacture its chips on the semiconductor industry’s existing high-volume production lines. The company is currently choosing a site for a production facility ahead of its rack deliveries to customers in 2028. Both Lumai and Neurophos are betting they’ll get their products to market before traditional CMOS can catch up to their energy savings. “Silicon will keep improving, but digital efficiency gains now come slowly and at rising cost,” Burr says. “Optics offers a different scaling relationship, in which efficiency improves as matrices grow. Larger models, longer context windows, and agentic workloads are all pushing prefill in that direction.” Bridging the gap on-chip Free-space optics carries the promise of almost energy-free multiplication, as in Goodman’s design. But another big advance in optics since Goodman’s work in the 1970s is integrated photonics, which allows you to guide and manipulate light on-chip. “The name of the game is to do as large a vector size as possible to maximize the benefit of using optics, and for that reason the free-space approaches are promising,” says Yale’s Logan Wright. “But it’s still fundamentally harder” to use the free-space approach, “because there’s just so much less infrastructure than in silicon photonics.” Other companies—like Shanghai-based Lightelligence and Q.ANT , based in Stuttgart, Germany—are trading the 3D advantage of free-space optics for the manufacturability of photonics integrated directly onto a silicon chip. “There is a good reason that free-space optics are usually limited to 1,000 units a year,” says Q.ANT’s CEO and founder, Michael Förtsch . “The reason for this is lens inspection, assembly strategy, and so on. Semiconductor-manufacturable integrated photonic circuits are at this point way more promising to reach volume production.” Vector-matrix multiplication with integrated photonics One way to do vector-matrix multiplication with light on-chip involves encoding vector elements into the amplitudes of pulses of light, traveling sequentially through a waveguide. The multiplication is performed by Mach-Zehnder interferometers: A waveguide splits in two, and the phase of light traveling through one of the paths is shifted by a controlled voltage. When the two paths reunite, the resulting light intensity depends on that phase shift, performing a multiplication. Encoding the matrix elements into the phase shifts turns this into vector-matrix multiplication. A photodetector then collects the light from all three pulses, performing the accumulation step. In Q.ANT’s approach, the input data is encoded into the phase and amplitude of light pulses via on-chip modulators. A vector in this scheme is represented as a sequence of such pulses, each representing one vector element. The light is guided around the chip with waveguides. The basic computational element is an interferometer: A waveguide splits into two paths, and the light beam traveling down one path is subjected to a phase shift, controlled by a set voltage. When the two paths recombine, the resulting interference performs a computation. Then, photodetectors and analog-to-digital converters turn the result back into digital data. The serialized vector-matrix multiplication approach is slower than Goodman’s computer, where the whole calculation happens at once. However, the slower speed can be mitigated by using multiple wavelengths at once, effectively encoding multiple vectors into light simultaneously. Q.ANT’s Native Processing Server is already being used in research institutions like the Leibniz Supercomputing Centre in Munich and the Jülich Supercomputing Centre in Jülich, both in Germany. Earlier this year, the company announced a commercial sale to the cloud provider Ionos. Similarly, Lightelligence’s PACE2 processor is capable of multiplying 128-by-128-element matrices. In a paper released in 2025, the company described vector-matrix multiplication at a 1-gigahertz frequency and 3-nanosecond latency, claiming two orders of magnitude lower latency than with traditional GPUs. The energy advantage is yet to be conclusively demonstrated, however, and Q.ANT’s Förtsch admits there is still a ways to go. The main issue is the energy cost of analog-to-digital conversion and back. As long as a fast, low-energy converter does not exist, Förtsch says, “we don’t see realistic chances that…a general vector-matrix multiplication machine in optics makes sense.” Beyond matrix-vector multiplication Not everyone in the field is focused on matrix-vector multiplication, despite it being all the rage in the AI inference world. In fact, while the optical vector-matrix multiply idea goes back to the 1970s, other computations with optics have been investigated as far back as the 1950s. For example, a Fourier transform—a common operation that decomposes a complex wave or signal into its constituent frequencies—can be done in optics with a single lens. “A digital chip has to approximate [Fourier transforms] in many small steps, using hundreds to thousands of transistors and more compute cycles,” says Q.ANT’s Förtsch. “Models that use such nonlinear functions can reach the same or better accuracy with fewer parameters and fewer operations.” Even though Q.ANT’s optical processor has been used for traditional vector-matrix multiplication, the company believes its greatest advantages lie in alternative AI architectures that leverage more complex functions. “Tasks such as image classification and segmentation rely heavily on operations like Fourier series, transformations, and other nonlinear functions, which photonics handles natively. We see similar potential in generative AI, especially image and video generation,” Förtsch says. The Israel-based startup LightSolver is also targeting algorithms that are a more natural fit for its device. “If you look at propagating electromagnetic waves, essentially, they are running differential equations in their nature,” says Ruti Ben-Shlomi , CEO and cofounder of LightSolver. She says differential equations can be solved much faster and with higher energy efficiency on the company’s laser processing unit (LPU) than on a traditional computer. LightSolver’s LPU is an interesting twist on the Goodman optical-computer design. It has input light, a programmable membrane in the form of a spatial light modulator, and output light, but the whole thing is placed in a cavity, where light bounces back and forth many times before reaching a steady state. In addition, the team places a gain medium inside the cavity. This gain medium functions much like those found inside a laser, causing the bouncing light to build up in intensity. LightSolver, a startup based in Israel, is using free-space optics to quickly solve differential equations by harnessing the natural properties of light. LightSolver Once a particular problem is encoded into the modulator, the gain medium is stimulated to emit random photons. They bounce back and forth, increasing in intensity when passing through the gain medium again, experiencing preprogrammed changes through the modulator and interacting with one another until they reach a steady state—the solution. Then, a simple camera takes a picture of the steady-state result. Using emulation, the LightSolver team recently showed that their LPU can solve differential equations 40 to 80,000 times as fast as a GPU, depending on the workflow. They are now working on explicitly benchmarking the energy improvements. LightSolver’s team is currently working on AI applications for its LPU as well, using the company’s own algorithm to do image generation from text. “We’re not doing vector-matrix multiplication very fast. We are doing something different. We need to assume that the way you train the model, and you then do inference, is completely different. But if you do it differently, you’ll be able to do image generation with dramatic energy-consumption decrease and speedup,” Ben-Shlomi says. LightSolver has a working prototype of its LPU, and the team is working on a larger, rack-mountable box. Computing in transit Yet another way to leverage light’s particular strengths is being pursued by Optalysys , a startup based in Leeds, England. Nick New , founder and chief product officer, has a background in free-space optics, and so he understood that taking a Fourier transform is very easy to do with light. The key idea behind Optalysys’s technology is taking that Fourier capability of optics in free space and making it work on-chip. “Rather than using a lens these days, we have our own component, which is a passive component in the plane of the silicon that does that same job,” New says. And by cleverly designing that component with multiple outputs, the team figured out how to perform different operations as well. “Because of how the Fourier transform response is generated, you can actually pull out different mathematical operations from it,” New says. “We can produce very large, high-precision digital functions at superhigh efficiencies, using our analog photonics approach.” “We’re effectively adding processing to where there is none right now.” —Nick New, Optalysis Instead of redesigning an accelerator from scratch, Optalysys is targeting a piece of the AI workload that’s often already in the optical domain: networking. In the data center, racks of computers are connected to each other with fiber optics, and the optical connections are increasingly getting closer and closer to the GPUs and CPUs themselves. Some computations already happen while the data is en route. These computations, which include combining results from multiple GPUs, are executed inside network switch cards. But the cards naturally use power to do that math. With passive optical components, these computations could be done essentially for free. New says that in addition to communication between GPUs, Optalysys’s technology could be used to facilitate a GPU’s communication with memory, doing things like compression and format conversion on the fly. Going back to AI inference, this approach could improve the decode part of the workload. Unlike prefill, decode is memory bound: The most costly part is shuffling model data in and out of memory. “We’re more focused on the memory-bound applications, which fits very well with this principle of adding processing into the communication path,” New says. “We’re effectively adding processing to where there is none right now.” The likely future of optical computing How likely are optical computers to replace GPUs in the data center? Yale’s Wright is not too optimistic. “The direction of algorithm development is not going to be a direction that is automatically favorable for optics,” he says. “In fact, it’s most likely to go in the opposite direction, because [AI model developers] want it to work better on GPUs.” However, even if our AI queries aren’t going to be computed in light in the next few years, that investment in the technology won’t be in vain. Says Wright, “The reason that I and many other people in the field are at least somewhat optimistic is that there’s real investment from companies like Nvidia and TSMC in developing co-packaged silicon photonics—not for computing, but for circuit switching and interconnects, and that just kind of opens the door to do a little bit more in the future.” Whether that technology ends up crunching vector-matrix multiplication, doing bespoke simulations, or performing in-network computations, the computing ecosystem seems ripe for a variety of approaches. “We see the data center of the future as heterogeneous: CPUs, GPUs and photonic NPUs [neural processing units] each take on the tasks they are best suited for,” says Q.ANT’s Förtsch. “Running each task on the most efficient hardware can significantly reduce energy use and operating costs.”

items.originalTitle: Is Watching Videos at 2x Speed a Bad Idea?
items.author: Veronique Greenwood
items.title: Is Watching Videos at 2x Speed a Bad Idea?
items.summary: —We Are / Getty Images In You Can See Everything , the documentary about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes and her husband Billy Evans, Evans is often seen busily watching videos on 2x speed . He’s not the only one; many people, especially younger ones , are playing video and audio content at faster speeds to get through the material more quickly. In 2022, a YouGov poll found that 11% of respondents reported having watched sped-up content, and in a 2024 paper, 84% of surveyed university students reported doing it with taped lectures. We asked researchers whether this is actually an effective way to learn. Does speeding content up make it harder to retain? With training, the human ear can handle some pretty impressive speeds, says Marcus Pearce, a cognitive scientist at Queen Mary University of London. “The average rate of speech is around 150-200 words per minute,” he says. “But we can understand speech up to about double that.” He describes a blind colleague who used screen reading software that read his emails aloud at about 400 to 500 words per minute, “which sounds like gobbledygook unless you're used to it,” he says. “There definitely is an effect of training. You can train your brain to do it.” A 2025 metanalysis of 24 studies looked at whether speeding up video lectures made people perform worse on assessments afterwards, and the authors concluded that up to 1.5x, there wasn’t much of a negative effect on people’s scores. Above 2x, the negative effect grew larger. “At two times playback speed, then memory performance is quite significantly impaired,” says Pearce, who wasn’t involved in the paper but wrote an analysis of it . “So if you go up to two and a half times, then on average it would be about a 17%” decline in scores. Pearce thinks this may have to do with working memory , the system we use to take in information, compare it to what we already know, and stash it in long-term memory. “Working memory importantly has a limited capacity,” he says. “So it can get overloaded if too much information comes in at one time.” Is there a way to make speeding through content more efficient? One way to help your brain retain information is to include video, slides with text, or images in the material you’re speeding through—in other words, to not just rely on sound for the information, says Ashley Chen, a cognitive psychologist at University of California, Los Angeles, who has authored articles on speed-watching and speed-listening. In one set of studies , “we saw that the audiovisual group actually significantly outperformed the audio-only group on a later test,” she says. “And interestingly, there were no differences in performance between the 1x- and 2x-speed audiovisual groups. So this suggests to us that pairing narration with some sort of visual component to learning can help mitigate the negative effects we see with accelerated playback speeds.” Taking notes while watching helps too, Chen and colleagues have found . People who took notes while watching at 2x speed performed better later on a quiz of the information than people who watched at 1x speed and took no notes. Will watching at 2x-speed negatively affect the brain? “The long-term effects I think are not really known,” says Pearce. “There's not really been much evidence scientifically.” While it’s outside the scope of her memory research, Chen says she understands why people might be worried. “On one hand, I think faster playback speed can potentially limit mind wandering, maybe encourage more sustained engagement of information,” she says, pointing to the work of her coauthor, Dillon Murphy, who has studied lecture speed and mind-wandering and found lower rates when watching videos faster. On the other hand, watching or listening at high speed might be more mentally taxing than at a normal speed, and it may affect people’s ability to sustain their attention when doing slower activities, she says. “As it stands, we don't yet have sufficient evidence to draw very strong conclusions about this. “But I do think it is a very interesting question,” she says, “especially as more and more individuals start accelerating playback speed, and maybe starting at an even younger age than our current generation of students.”

items.originalTitle: Yesteryear Became a Cultural Sensation. Caro Claire Burke Is Still Reeling
items.author: Lucy Feldman
items.title: Yesteryear Became a Cultural Sensation. Caro Claire Burke Is Still Reeling
items.summary: The nurses in the labor and delivery unit at a Boston-area hospital were in for a surprise. On the Wednesday in September when their book club was scheduled to discuss Caro Claire Burke ’s Yesteryear , the author herself showed up to deliver her first child. Which is how, in the heady aftermath of giving birth, Burke found herself propped up in her hospital bed, signing copies of her novel. It was as surreal a scene as any from a year in which she went from relative obscurity to the center of the cultural conversation. Sitting on her living-room couch five weeks later, watching as her husband feeds their infant, all tiny limbs and milk-bloated belly, Burke reflects on the moment. “Holy sh-t,” she remembers thinking. “This has permeated.” The woman who wrote the most divisive mother character in fiction this year is now in the thralls of new motherhood herself, still recovering physically and already deeply in love with her child. Her experience has been nothing like that of Natalie Heller Mills, the protagonist of her best seller, who enters this phase of life entirely unprepared and furious at a world determined to keep her contained. “I will never be Natalie again,” the character narrates. “I will only ever be Mama.” For Burke, this change is only one of the universe-shifting transitions she’s experienced recently. When she sold her novel two years ago to Knopf—in a seven-figure deal, which is rare for a debut—her financial reality transformed completely. She paid off her car loan, bought this house in coastal Massachusetts, the region where she grew up, and became someone who could independently afford to write fiction for a living. Around the same time, she launched a podcast, Diabolical Lies , with Katie Gatti Tassin, establishing herself as a feminist cultural critic. And this year, Burke achieved her lifelong dream of becoming a published novelist—only to see her spiky, overtly political novel become a sensational hit. —Tonje Thilesen for TIME Buy your copy of the 100 Must-Read Books of 2026 issue here The impact of Yesteryear , published in April, cannot be overstated. The novel has sold 3.5 million copies around the world. Even before you crack the spine, it offers an enticing package: a strong title, the investment of one of the most powerful imprints in American publishing, an early endorsement from Anne Hathaway—who is set to produce and star in an adaptation from Amazon MGM Studios—and the tightest, most delicious elevator pitch for a literary novel in recent memory: a tradwife influencer wakes up in 1855 and is forced to actually live the lifestyle she’s been selling online. Read more about Caro Claire Burke in the 100 Must-Read Books of 2026 A twisty thriller with a biting voice, it’s the kind of book that you have to discuss with someone else as soon as you finish, and it has soared to zeitgeist-defining status à la Gillian Flynn’s Gone Girl , R.F. Kuang’s Yellowface , and Sally Rooney’s Normal People . This year, it has become, alongside Belle Burden’s divorce memoir Strangers and Lena Dunham’s Famesick , one of the few books that seemingly everyone is talking about. Good Morning America selected it as their April book club pick. In May, Burke was a guest on Late Night With Seth Meyers , one of only a handful of novelists to appear on the show in 2026. These days, authors are lucky to make book-tour stops in a few cities, but Burke has visited 30, and, after a maternity break, is set to continue on to Australia, New Zealand, and multiple countries in Europe. Women dressed as Natalie for Halloween, recruiting friends to go as her chickens, her cows, her useless husband Caleb. The premise of the book was recently a clue on Jeopardy! Regardless of a given reader’s politics, Yesteryear , which interrogates the virtues of a certain type of womanhood, touches a nerve. Some have read it as a rebuke of conservative ideals—Natalie, who comes from a Christian fundamentalist community, is miserable, therefore Burke must be saying that women who desire “traditional” lives are doomed. Others have read it as equally harsh on liberals—the women in the novel who tout progressive values are just as screwed. Some have accused Burke of taking a lazy shortcut, not doing enough research to articulate Natalie’s specific religious sect; others have perceived a deeper point about gender and control in that choice. Many think Natalie is atrocious, morally bad, and unrelatable; many also see her as a sympathetic victim. Burke, as the author who created this character and this world, has been accused of hating women herself. "People had really strong opinions about the book before it even came out,” she says. “A lot of the criticism I will see, sometimes it's very legitimate—like the pacing was off or whatever—and sometimes it's literally just this book was supposed to be something else." Burke likens her experience of the seven months since publication to being blasted into space on a rocket ship. “There have been moments where it's like we are hurtling through the atmosphere, and I'm pretty sure we are not going to make it through,” she says. Now she can finally exhale. It’s striking that assuming a new identity as a mother and marching through the sleepless first weeks with a brand-new baby could ever be considered a respite. But the time with her family has brought her back to herself. “I feel like a normal person again,” Burke says, “and I want to try to keep that.” One of the first things Burke posted on social media after Yesteryear became an instant best seller was a slideshow of rejection notices from editors, residency programs, literary magazines, and more: I just wanted more concept and plot… I’m not quite caught up in the narrative… ...lost momentum… Hers is the kind of success that’s so striking that people assume it’s a fluke—that the writer behind Yesteryear struck gold right out of the gate. But Burke is the first person to emphasize just how long and hard she worked to be published—and how many disappointments she faced along the way. Even now she’s been turned down for ideas and events she’s pitched. “I just wanted to encourage writers to remember that it's never not bumpy,” she says, “and that the rejection you're receiving doesn't mean you might not end up with a Yesteryear . In fact, it probably means that's the only way that you get there.” Burke tried to establish her career as an author for a full decade before the Yesteryear boom. After attempting a premed track at the University of Virginia (which she let go after getting a C in chemistry) and considering law school (she took the LSAT and never even looked at her score), Burke committed to writing, earning an MFA from Bennington College. She freelanced, publishing essays and short stories, and completed two novels that never sold. Her only full-time job was from 2022 to 2024 as an editor at Katie Couric Media, where she churned out editorial and branded articles. After the second novel was rejected in 2023, she had a reality-check moment. Her husband, Riley Strand, had been covering their finances for years. But they wanted kids, and Burke was 30, so she decided to focus on her job and take a break from fiction. On a whim, she downloaded TikTok, where she was fed a stream of videos by tradwife influencers—women who showcase their lifestyles conforming to traditional gender roles—and started posting her own videos analyzing their meaning. Suddenly, people cared what she had to say, and soon she connected with Tassin, with whom she’d launch the podcast. She also had the idea for her next attempt at a novel. Burke wrote the first draft of Yesteryear in two feverish months, surprising herself with the wickedly funny, cutting voice of Natalie Heller Mills. Natalie is an acidic, vitriolic rural Idahoan who grows up sheltered but curious about the world. She heads to Harvard to have her mind expanded, only to find that her liberal peers are just as oppressed in their own way, and decides to retreat to the familiar safety of marriage, motherhood, and a life led by her husband. Eventually, she lobbies her politico father-in-law to buy them a farm, which she uses to create a picturesque vision of a “traditional” life for millions of followers on social media, one abundant with barn animals, homemade dinners, and a gaggle of homeschooled tots—never revealing the help they have behind the scenes. She becomes a conservative icon, held up in the manosphere as the ideal woman: “Look how exhausted and beautiful she is.” And then one day, Natalie wakes up in the mid-19th century, and gone are the luxuries of modern wealth. Her performance becomes her reality, and she needs to find out how—and why—or else risk being stuck in her new hell forever. —Tonje Thilesen for TIME After a 12-way bidding war, Burke sold the novel in 2024 to Knopf editorial director of fiction Jenny Jackson, who had twice tried to acquire it before anyone else could make an offer. That was a first for Jackson, the editor of heavy hitters like Kevin Kwan and Emily St. John Mandel . “I personally lose some sleep any time I spend seven figures on a book, and if it’s an author with no track record whatsoever, it’s extra scary,” she says. Once the book went to auction, she was encouraged to see that it wasn’t just literary imprints like hers that wanted Yesteryear , but commercial ones too—Viking, Simon & Schuster, Avid Reader, Crown, Dutton, and Atria all came to the table. “All of these publishers have a vision for how they could do this book, so that means there are a lot of different kinds of bookshelves it could fit on,” Jackson recalls thinking. “And that means we have a hit.” Jackson feels like she’s witnessed the birth of a public intellectual. Because Burke and Tassin began building an audience before the book came out, Burke arrived as a debut novelist with a ready-made fan base. “We had this launch event with maybe 700 attendees—completely sold out for a debut—and all the young women were wearing Diabolical Lies T-shirts,” Jackson says. “When we signed up this book, we were signing up a debut novel, and what we have on our hands now is a very prominent American thinker.” For his part, Strand says he was happy to wait for the industry to catch on to his wife’s talents—but he remembers one moment that gave him pause. Bouncing their child in his arms, he shares a family secret: “Caroline watches reality TV while she writes.” He smiles at Burke, who laughs. “I will go on the record saying I always believed in you, but there was a time where Caroline was writing while watching TV, and I walked in, and I was like, maybe she's not going to make it.” At a local general store, Burke is greeted with a hug by the manager. She orders a latte and carries it outside to a picnic table. She looks like any 33-year-old taking a coffee break on a crisp fall day. But you can see it on her face, hear it in the way she pauses to think before she speaks—she exists in a liminal space between her old identity of Caroline and her new one as the artist behind a cultural phenomenon. Earlier in the day, she went to get her eyebrows waxed, and when the esthetician asked what she does for a living, she said she was a writer—then lied and told the woman she self-publishes romance novels. “I have brain bleeds every time I have to map my novel life onto my home life,” she says. “I feel like I’m constantly glitching. Everyone’s fine and normal, and I’m the one who’s making it weird.” She never envisioned Yesteryear being the kind of book that such a wide audience would engage with. Ann Patchett, Taylor Jenkins Reid, Emily Henry, Virginia Evans—she lists authors whose work is hugely commercial yet generally not “contentious.” “ Yesteryear has so many hot-button things,” she says. “There’s almost a dissonance between what it is and the level that it reached.” Similarly, Burke never imagined that she herself would become part of the story. She and Tassin had talked before the book was published about how any woman who’s put on a pedestal will inevitably face backlash. “The second half of that play is knocking her down off of it,” Tassin says. “So when all the initial coverage was so glowing, we were like, ‘Oh god. It’s coming.’” But it wasn’t just that people were suggesting that Burke had cashed in on a viral trend or questioning whether the book lived up to the hype, which was difficult enough. “There were many times throughout the last year where I was like, ‘This book totally failed. People hate it. People hate me. The sales are fraudulent. I’m an industry plant. I guess everyone’s right, and the book is awful, and I failed upwards,’” Burke says, noting that there was a period when she couldn’t log into Substack to work on Diabolical Lies because she was tagged in so many “takedown” posts. People also wanted her to explain exactly how her character’s life and beliefs mirrored her own. Tassin refers to the book’s reception as “ Yesteryear extended performance art,” an ironic recreation of the very dynamics that Natalie faces when her online presence becomes so big that people begin treating her as an object up for debate. Burke is good at social media—this whole chapter started with her drawing a crowd for sharing her opinions online, and she regularly posts snappy responses to commentators. But she’s conflicted about the ways in which she’s now exposed. She wants to keep her personal world, particularly anything having to do with her child, as private as possible. “People started to talk about my pregnancy in the narrative of Yesteryear , which is pretty uncomfortable,” she says. She also emphasizes that that part of her life is not relevant to her work. “That’s a political feeling I have about all of the ways in which my experience has been so gendered—of how people have perceived the book, how they talk about me as an author, how they treat female authors—and I’m like, ‘No. You don’t do this with men,’” she says. “It is possible for me to write about children and motherhood, and for you to not know about how I am a mother in my private life.” At the same time, Burke knows there’s no changing the fact that she’s chosen to put her views out there, which makes them fair game for conversation. She has talked about the fact that she was raised Catholic with conservative values and voted for Mitt Romney in 2012 before evolving her perspective. On Diabolical Lies , she and Tassin have dissected everything from MAGA figures like Karoline Leavitt and Charlie Kirk to Hollywood’s obsession with thinness. Still, she wants to draw a line between herself as a person and the art she creates. For anyone seeking to read Yesteryear as a manifesto, “I don’t think they’ll find anything coherent,” she says. That ambiguity, the way it refuses to take sides, has helped the book travel. “Most people come away with totally different takes on the moral of the story, and that to me is why people want to talk about it.” Jackson invented a phrase during their time editing the novel that Burke often repeats as the guiding theme of her work: “the grand performance of womanhood.” It speaks to the way women are always being watched and evaluated on how well we are playing our roles. Yesteryear suggests not only that women are set up to fail but also that this surveillance can be so powerful it becomes ingrained in our sense of self. “The idea of Natalie being a good or bad person is so boring to me, and it’s so beside the point,” Burke says. “But why Natalie operates the way that she does, and why she is constantly surveilling herself and second-guessing her thoughts—it’s relevant to fundamentalism, but it’s also relevant to just being a woman.” If there’s one reader takeaway that Burke agrees with, it’s that neither the tradwife or the girl-boss model is working. “There really is no one correct way to be a woman,” she says. “If you're conservative or liberal, no matter what, you often have to deal with choices that are not ideal.” Burke is still trying to make sense of all the noise. People frequently ask her how she feels about “the discourse,” and she’s come to realize that there are so many threads of debate, she can never assume which one an individual is referring to. “It’s like their algorithm. They’re either like, ‘How are you holding up? I know everyone hates your book,’ or they're like, ‘Oh my God, you're going to win a Pulitzer, right?’” She wrote Yesteryear as if no one was watching, because no one was. She was fearless, reckless. “That’s why it was so much fun to write—and I also think that’s why it’s good,” she says. Now she’s under a microscope. “I feel like, well, you don’t want to say the wrong thing. But with Yesteryear I said every wrong thing.” Her goal, she insists, is not to replicate the success of her debut. She doesn’t ever want to be a viral topic on social media again, and she doesn’t need to make another appearance on late-night TV. “I just want to write books, which sounds really corny, but being in the center of the zeitgeist is very uncomfortable,” she says. She names Patchett, Rooney, and Maggie O’Farrell as writers whose careers she looks to as the model, women who publish consistently and have a following of readers who will take the time to pick up their new releases. Maybe people love your latest book, maybe they don’t—but they’ll keep giving you another chance. —Tonje Thilesen for TIME Burke will happily leave behind the kinds of debates that she’s been brought into with Yesteryear : whether America is reading enough, whether the books that are getting read are any good, whether social media has broken the publishing industry. After experiencing firsthand the way purported book fans gleefully smack down the ones that become hits, she can only point out how self-defeating that pattern is, continue to write what inspires her, and hope readers want to check out the new Caro Claire Burke, whatever that turns out to be. “The same people who have said so many things about my book are the people who complain that no one reads,” she says. “I'm like, ‘Well, 2 million people just read this. Does that count?’” So how does she deal with the sky-high expectations Yesteryear has created? A little realism. “We’ll all be dead someday. I remind myself that frequently. I’ll be dead someday, and none of this will matter,” she says, smiling. As hard as it’s been for her to process everything that has happened with Yesteryear , it’s not hard for her to be grateful she’s been established as someone who has something to say. “The worst thing in the world is silence. Dude, I tried—I was writing silently for a decade. That’s way worse,” she says. “So as much as I have to deal with my own paranoia and neuroses now, I also have an agent. I have a publishing team. I have the money to take time to write. I have people who care if I write something next. That’s such a privilege.” And write something she will: Burke and Jackson reveal exclusively to TIME that they’ve signed a deal for Burke’s next novel. “Her idea is the kind of thing where you say the sentence, and you're like, Oh, yeah,” Jackson says. She bought the book based on the concept alone. items.originalTitle: Want to Feel Happier? Spend $5 on Someone Else
items.author: Angela Haupt
items.title: Want to Feel Happier? Spend $5 on Someone Else
items.summary: —Photo-Illustration by TIME (Source Images: Billion Photos, Canvalutionaries, Layer-Lab, aliaksandrbarysenka, Pexels and Sync Std via Canva) If someone handed you $5 and told you to buy whatever would make you happiest, who would you spend it on? If you said “yourself,” well, that’s a pretty tempting answer. Your favorite coffee would surely turn your morning around; a chocolate croissant wouldn’t hurt, either. And research suggests that most people tend to think they’d get the biggest happiness boost by spending money on themselves. Yet treating someone else might leave you feeling even better. Researchers who study generosity have found that spending a few dollars on another person can be a surprisingly effective way to boost your own mood—no extravagant gift or special occasion required. “It’s less about the specific dollar amount and more about how you do it,” says Elizabeth Dunn, a psychologist at the University of British Columbia in Canada who studies spending and happiness. She suggests asking yourself: “Is this what this person needs right now?” So what makes a small purchase rewarding for everyone involved? We asked experts how to put a few dollars to good use. Why spending money on others can make you happier In a 2008 study , researchers gave people $5 or $20 and told them to spend it that day either on themselves or on someone else. When they checked in later that evening, those assigned to spend on others were happier. Spending $20 didn’t produce a bigger happiness boost than spending $5. People weren’t making grand gestures, recalls study co-author Lara Aknin, a social psychologist at Simon Fraser University in British Columbia. They were bringing pizza home to their family, treating a friend to coffee, or buying a toy for a sibling. “These were just really small but thoughtful gestures,” she says. Since then, she and her colleagues have explored whether the benefits extend beyond North America. In a paper drawing on survey data from 136 countries , they found that charitable giving was associated with greater happiness in both wealthy and poorer countries. Why might giving feel so good? Consider what you’re getting along with the satisfaction of picking out a treat someone will love: a reason to stop by their desk, invite them out, or let them know you’ve been thinking about them. The purchase might be small, but it gives you an opening to connect. “One of the reasons I think giving makes us happy is because it builds and sustains these relationships that are so important for our well-being,” Aknin says. From an evolutionary perspective, she points out, people depended on one another for food, safety, and survival. We still need other people—and she suspects that helping feels rewarding in part because it encourages us to maintain social connections. “These small everyday acts of giving help signal to other people and to ourselves that we have these meaningful relationships in our lives,” she says. Her research suggests that the interaction itself can be an important ingredient. In studies she conducted with Dunn and other colleagues, spending on friends or acquaintances was most emotionally rewarding when it created an opportunity for social connection. Buying someone coffee, for example, can also buy you a few minutes together. “You’re not only there for the gift-giving exchange, but you get some extra face time with this person that you care about,” Aknin says. “The togetherness really matters.” Small gestures can make people feel seen and appreciated, adds Alexis Sturnick, a licensed clinical social worker and founder of Resilience Therapy Group in New York. Remembering that your friend likes a particular tea tells them you’ve been listening; showing up with a cup tells them you remembered. The recipient might protest that they haven’t done anything to deserve it. “That’s kind of the point,” Sturnick says. “You didn’t need to.” There doesn’t have to be an occasion—or a favor you’re repaying—to show someone they matter to you. The best ways to spend $5 on someone else Maybe your coworker’s having a miserable day, and you know exactly how she takes her coffee. Or you spot a candy bar your friend loved as a kid and pick one up for her. “Thoughtfulness maybe matters a little bit more than the sheer amount of money that you’re spending,” Dunn says. Dunn’s husband recently decided they were going to be that house on Halloween—the one handing out full-size candy bars. They stocked up at Costco, then got to watch the trick-or-treaters discover their good fortune. “The expressions of surprise and delight from children, young and old, put me in the best mood,” she says. “It was like the best use of money.” You don’t have to wait for a holiday to surprise someone. Bring your partner their favorite snack or show up with a treat for a friend you haven’t seen in a while. Thinking about what someone else would enjoy can also get you out of your own head, Sturnick says. Maybe you’ve spent the morning replaying an awkward conversation. Now, instead, you’re wondering whether your friend will be home if you stop by. “We’re on our computer, we’re in our phone, we’re all dealing with our own things,” she says. “It’s sometimes hard to remember to step outside of it.” If you’d rather donate your $5, choose a cause you care about and look for an explanation of what your contribution helps accomplish. In a study by Aknin, Dunn, and colleagues, people who donated larger amounts reported greater happiness—but only when the charity explained how their money would make a difference. That might mean knowing your donation will help provide meals for families facing food insecurity, or cover the cost of spaying or neutering rescue cats. You don’t have to meet the recipients to feel good about giving, Dunn says—but you should have a clear idea of where your money is going. “We’re more likely to find joy in giving if we can directly observe or at least vividly imagine how our generosity is actually making a difference,” she says. How to make giving a habit without overspending One of Aknin’s friends has a simple way to remember to treat other people: Each week, she sets aside a $5 bill in her wallet. Then she waits for an opportunity to spend it on someone else. Sometimes that’s a friend; sometimes it’s a stranger. Aknin hasn’t studied her friend’s particular routine, but says one way to make giving more rewarding is to “feel like you’ve had a choice in how you do it,” including who you treat, when, and how. If you’re setting aside money regularly, Dunn suggests varying how you use it. Treat a friend one week; pick out something small for your partner the next. She hasn’t directly tested that strategy, she notes, but changing the experience may help keep it enjoyable rather than automatic. Sturnick suggests naming the fund so you remember what you’re saving for. You could label a jar “just because” or add a “treat someone” category to your budget. Choose an amount that fits your finances, whether that means setting aside $1 a week or collecting spare change until you have enough to buy someone a coffee. If spending would add stress, try a free gesture instead: Hold the door, check in on a friend, or take a moment to thank someone who’s helped you. “It doesn’t have to be monetary,” Sturnick says. “It goes a really, really long way.” Even when you can afford it, giving can start to feel like something you have to keep up with. Sturnick sends Mother’s Day flowers to several people in her life, and now sometimes worries about how they’d feel if she stopped. Would they think she’d forgotten them? Would someone feel hurt? “It could be reversed and become this unnecessary stress or resentment that you’re only then putting on yourself,” she says. Remember: Buying someone coffee once doesn’t mean you have to pick up the tab every time. The amount you can spare might change, too. Give yourself credit for what you can do, Sturnick says: “I’m doing the little bit that I can today, and it’s enough.”

items.originalTitle: DESI weighs the Milky Way more precisely than ever
items.author: Sam Jarman
items.title: DESI weighs the Milky Way more precisely than ever
items.summary: To estimate the Milky Way's mass, astronomers need to track the movements of stars and smaller satellite galaxies under its gravitational pull. The faster these objects travel at a given distance, the more mass is needed to hold them in place. For some time, these measurements have shown that most of our galaxy's mass can't be accounted for by the stars and gas we can see. However, they have also produced estimates that differ widely.
